A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same quantization study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content and renumbered tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of five models across five benchmarks, supplemented by judge-validation results, case studies, and statistical analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these original benchmark experiments, judge-validation results, case studies, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: The quantization procedures, SmoothQuant adaptation for Llama-3.1 70B, and YaRN context extension are retained. Expanded implementation explanations in Appendix A do not establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate RULER, ONERULER, NOCHA, FACTSCORE, and CS4 with the same retrieval, reasoning, and generation coverage, including the same 26-language evaluation.

E2.justification: The matched comparisons retain BF16 and the same five quantized configurations: FP8, GPTQ-int8, AWQ-int4, GPTQ-int4, and BNB-nf4. No comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Model configurations, evaluation sample sizes, context lengths, decoding, metrics, and judging procedures are retained. The calibration settings newly specified in Table 1 document existing configurations rather than establish protocol changes.

E4.justification: The context-length, language, task-difficulty, bias, abstention, and constraint analyses remain, as do the 42 judge-validation evaluations and appendix examples. Proposed calibration remedies in v3 are explicitly left for future evaluation.

E5.justification: Appendix F retains the mixed-effects analyses, confidence intervals, standard errors, and Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons. Its statistical content matches after table renumbering; no run-count, seed, or uncertainty-reporting practice is added.

E6.justification: Appendix A.3 newly reports estimated compute consumption by benchmark, totaling roughly 5,800 GPU hours. This adds quantitative resource-use information; the benchmark scores, rankings, case-study outputs, and statistical results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The accuracy-difference and bias definitions and mixed-model formulations are retained. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs, and the expanded calibration discussion adds no formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: generally robust 8-bit quantization, greater long-context and multilingual degradation at 4 bits, and substantial dependence on model and task.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds a caveat that AWQ/GPTQ models from different providers may use different calibration sets. It also proposes long-context, multilingual, and attention calibration as possible remedies, extending the existing RoPE-error hypothesis without testing these explanations.

D1.justification: New Table 1 supplies specific checkpoint links and additional grouping, scaling, damping, and calibration details. Appendix A expands the bitsandbytes loading explanation and adds per-benchmark compute estimates, improving documentation of the retained setup.

R1.justification: v3 adds Williams and Aletras (2023) on calibration data and Hsieh et al. (2024b) on positional attention calibration. These support proposed remedies; the central positioning against prior quantization evaluations remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Selected introduction and results paragraphs are rewritten, Appendix A.1 is reorganized around the source table, and computational-cost and explanatory passages are added. The overall narrative structure remains intact; acknowledgments also expand.

P2.justification: v3 adds the model-source table and adjusts captions, figure placement, and appendix layout. Existing plots are retained. Statistical prose is enlarged, while the final CS4 post-hoc table is reduced in size, making it less legible.

improvement.justification: Table 1 and Appendix A improve implementation transparency and resource reporting, while the new calibration caveat qualifies comparisons between model families. These are useful, limited gains to an otherwise unchanged empirical study, outweighing the small readability loss from shrinking the final statistical table.
